title: Speak to him gently
hook: Allah sends Musa and Harun to Pharaoh and tells them to speak gently

segments.voice: Yesterday: wazir, the helper Musa asked for before the hardest meeting of his life. Your line was expand my chest.

You know the fantasy. The person who hurt you, the impossible boss, the relative who says the worst thing at every holiday, and you finally get your moment. You've rehearsed it in the shower a hundred times. Now take the worst person in the Qur'an. Pharaoh. He killed babies. He called himself a god. He enslaved a whole people. Musa and Harun are about to walk into his court with the backing of the Lord of the worlds. If anyone ever had permission to let someone have it, surely it's now. Then they get their instructions.
screen: `THE SPEECH YOU'VE REHEARSED.` → `THE WORST MAN IN THE STORY.` → `THEIR INSTRUCTIONS.`

segments.voice: Surah Ta-Ha. Go, you and your brother, with My signs, and don't grow slack in remembering Me. Go, both of you, to Pharaoh. He has transgressed all bounds. And speak to him a gentle word, that perhaps he may take heed, or feel some fear. The Arabic is qawlan layyinan: a soft word, a pliable word, the kind that bends instead of breaks. The command doesn't pretend Pharaoh is a good man. And still: gently. The verse gives the reason: perhaps he may take heed. Gentleness leaves a door open. A shout closes it. Muslim teachers have drawn a lesson from this for centuries, and it's often repeated: if Musa, one of the greatest prophets, was told to speak gently to Pharaoh, one of the worst of men, then how should we speak to each other, none of us as good as Musa, and none of those we argue with as bad as Pharaoh? Then Musa and Harun say what anyone would: our Lord, we're afraid he'll rush at us, or go too far. And the answer: don't be afraid. I am with you both. I hear, and I see. So the gentleness isn't weakness. They aren't soft because they're scared. They've been told they're not alone, and that frees them to be kind to a tyrant. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said something that fits right alongside: in a hadith in Sahih Muslim, he said gentleness is never in a thing without making it beautiful, and never taken from a thing without making it ugly.
screen: `HE HAS TRANSGRESSED.` · `SPEAK TO HIM A GENTLE WORD.` · `PERHAPS HE MAY TAKE HEED.` · `I AM WITH YOU BOTH.` · then, large: `QAWLAN LAYYINAN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you find hard, a medium one, not the hardest, and a true sentence you'd like to say to them, the one with some edge on it. Without making it false, soften it: take out the word that stings, add their name, leave a door open at the end, and say it quietly until it sounds like you. If you pray, you can ask for a gentle word.
Qawlan layyinan, a gentle word: what Musa and Harun were told to speak even to Pharaoh, so a door might stay open.
Your line: gently, even to pharaoh. Gentle, and not afraid of him. Tomorrow, the magicians.

howItsDone: Muslim teachers often cite the command to speak gently to Pharaoh (Qur'an 20:44) as the model for how to speak to anyone, especially in disagreement or when inviting others to faith.

fork.reveal: speak to him a gentle word, that perhaps he may take heed or fear. gentleness leaves a door open, even for Pharaoh.

original.note: Arabic, from Qur'an 20:44: "a gentle word" — soft, pliable speech.

trapdoor: what you thought: be nice to people who are nice.
what it means: even to Pharaoh, a tyrant the text says has transgressed, Musa and Harun are told to speak gently, so that he might take heed.
what a scholar hears: layyin is soft, yielding, the opposite of harsh; the "perhaps" in 20:44 is read by commentators as keeping the door open from Musa's side.
recall: the House in Mecca Muslims face to pray
